# Network diagnosis {.unnumbered}

When `dodgr` (@sec-m4-roteamento) returns `NA` for a route, or a distance matrix
comes out full of holes, the problem is almost never in the routing function: it is in the **network**.
Pieces of the network that do not connect to the rest, roads that cross without a shared node, one-way
stretches that lead into a dead end. This page is a complete case study, with module 4's
São Paulo–Santos network: the diagnosis of each problem, the maps that show where it
is, and the solutions, compared at the end.

It is reproducible from start to finish: every block is run when the site is built, and
the same code runs on your machine from the course folder. It takes about 4 minutes.

```{r}
#| message: false
library(dplyr)
library(sf)
library(dodgr)

dodgr::dodgr_cache_off()   # the graph is edited along the page: no cache, no surprises

crs_metrico <- 31983       # SIRGAS 2000 / UTM 23S: distances in metres in the SP region

# empty map, framed on the data, with the height used on the site
mapa_base <- function(dados, altura = "525px") {
  mapgl::maplibre(style = mapgl::carto_style("positron"), bounds = dados, height = altura)
}
```

## 1. Reading and cleaning the network

The network is the one from the routing chapter: OSM's main roads (from `motorway` to
`secondary`) in a rectangle between São Paulo and Santos.

```{r}
arquivo_rede <- "dados/brutos/rede_sao_paulo_santos.gpkg"

# the rectangle of the OSM query; it is also the edge of the study area
retangulo <- c(xmin = -46.80, ymin = -24.02, xmax = -46.25, ymax = -23.45)

if (!file.exists(arquivo_rede)) {
  # slow download (several minutes): the file usually already comes in the data package
  osmdata::set_overpass_url("https://overpass.kumi.systems/api/interpreter")

  res <- osmdata::opq(bbox = unname(retangulo), timeout = 300) |>
    osmdata::add_osm_feature(key = "highway", value = c(
      "motorway", "motorway_link", "trunk", "trunk_link", "primary", "primary_link",
      "secondary", "secondary_link")) |>
    osmdata::osmdata_sf()

  res$osm_lines |>
    dplyr::select(dplyr::any_of(c("osm_id", "name", "ref", "highway", "maxspeed",
                                  "oneway", "lanes"))) |>
    sf::st_write(arquivo_rede, quiet = TRUE)
}

rede_bruta <- sf::st_read(arquivo_rede, quiet = TRUE) |>
  dplyr::rename(geometry = geom)

table(rede_bruta$oneway, useNA = "ifany")
```

The basic cleaning fixes what would make `dodgr` complain or go wrong silently:

```{r}
rede <- rede_bruta |>
  # empty or invalid geometries break weight_streetnet()
  dplyr::filter(!sf::st_is_empty(geometry)) |>
  sf::st_make_valid() |>
  # the same OSM way should not appear twice
  dplyr::distinct(osm_id, .keep_all = TRUE) |>
  # dodgr only understands oneway = "yes"/"no"; "alternating" (direction that alternates during
  # the day) and empty become "no", that is, two-way
  dplyr::mutate(oneway = dplyr::if_else(oneway %in% "yes", "yes", "no"))

# if st_make_valid() produced MULTILINESTRING or collections, split into LINESTRING
if (!all(sf::st_geometry_type(rede) == "LINESTRING")) {
  rede <- rede |>
    sf::st_collection_extract("LINESTRING") |>
    sf::st_cast("LINESTRING", warn = FALSE)
}

c(trechos_brutos = nrow(rede_bruta), trechos_tratados = nrow(rede))
table(rede$oneway)
```

On this network, the cleaning discards no segment; what changes is the `oneway` column, which
no longer has values that `dodgr` does not understand.

The edge of the study area is the query rectangle, not the network's own bounding box: OSM
returns whole ways, including what goes past the limit.

```{r}
area_estudo <- sf::st_bbox(retangulo, crs = sf::st_crs(4326)) |>
  sf::st_as_sfc() |>
  sf::st_transform(crs_metrico)
borda <- sf::st_cast(area_estudo, "MULTILINESTRING")
borda_mapa <- sf::st_sf(geometry = sf::st_transform(borda, 4326))   # for the maps

# distance to the edge; a point outside the rectangle counts as "on the edge"
dist_borda <- function(pontos) {
  d <- as.numeric(sf::st_distance(pontos, borda))
  fora <- !lengths(sf::st_intersects(pontos, area_estudo))
  ifelse(fora, 0, d)
}
```

## 2. Building the graph and counting the pieces

```{r}
grafo <- dodgr::weight_streetnet(rede, wt_profile = "motorcar", type_col = "highway")

arestas_por_comp <- table(grafo$component)
length(arestas_por_comp)                               # how many components
head(sort(arestas_por_comp, decreasing = TRUE), 8)     # edges in the largest ones
```

The `component` column says which connected piece each edge belongs to; component 1 is always
the largest. The network has `r length(arestas_por_comp)` components, and the main one holds
`r format(round(100 * arestas_por_comp[["1"]] / nrow(grafo), 2))`% of the
edges. The rest are loose pieces: few in edges, but each is a place from which no
route leaves.

## 3. Where the loose pieces are, and why

For each vertex of the loose pieces, we measure the distance to the nearest vertex of the
main component and to the edge of the study area:

```{r}
vertices <- dodgr::dodgr_vertices(grafo) |>
  sf::st_as_sf(coords = c("x", "y"), crs = 4326, remove = FALSE) |>
  sf::st_transform(crs_metrico)

principal <- dplyr::filter(vertices, component == 1)
soltos    <- dplyr::filter(vertices, component > 1)

mais_proximo <- sf::st_nearest_feature(soltos, principal)
soltos$dist_principal <- as.numeric(sf::st_distance(soltos, principal[mais_proximo, ],
                                                    by_element = TRUE))
soltos$id_principal <- principal$id[mais_proximo]
soltos$dist_borda   <- dist_borda(soltos)
```

And we join the network's lines to each component, to see the road type and length, and to
test whether the loose piece **crosses** the main one without sharing a node:

```{r}
# the network lines (with geometry, type and road name) that make up the requested components
vias_malha <- dplyr::select(rede, way_id = osm_id, highway, name, geometry)

linhas_por_comp <- function(comps) {
  # each OSM way (way_id) appears once per component
  vias_comp <- grafo |>
    dplyr::filter(component %in% comps) |>
    dplyr::distinct(way_id, component)

  vias_comp |>
    dplyr::left_join(vias_malha, by = "way_id") |>
    sf::st_as_sf() |>
    sf::st_transform(crs_metrico)
}

linhas_soltas    <- linhas_por_comp(unique(soltos$component))
linhas_principal <- linhas_por_comp(1)

linhas_soltas$cruza <- lengths(sf::st_intersects(linhas_soltas, linhas_principal)) > 0
```

With these measures, each piece gets a **likely cause**, tested in this order:

| Cause | Rule | Solution |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Cut at the edge | less than 500 m from the edge | download OSM with a margin and crop afterwards |
| Near-coincident ends | less than 5 m from the main component | snap the ends together |
| Road outside the profile or the download | less than 300 m from the main component | download more road types, or create a connector |
| Crosses without a node | crosses the main component with no shared vertex | in OSM, it is an overpass (do not connect); outside OSM, create the nodes |
| Isolated | none of the above | a connector, if it makes sense, or discard |

The summary combines three tables, all with one row per loose component. We build each one
separately and then join them.

The first comes from the **vertices**: how many there are and how close the piece gets to the main component and to the
edge (the shortest distance among its vertices):

```{r}
por_vertices <- soltos |>
  sf::st_drop_geometry() |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    vertices         = dplyr::n(),
    dist_principal_m = min(dist_principal),
    dist_borda_m     = min(dist_borda),
    .by = component
  )
```

The second comes from the network's **lines**: the road types in the piece and how many of its lines cross
the main component:

```{r}
por_linhas <- linhas_soltas |>
  sf::st_drop_geometry() |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    vias        = paste(sort(unique(highway)), collapse = ", "),
    cruzamentos = sum(cruza),
    .by = component
  )
```

The third comes from the **graph**: the number of edges and the length. The graph has both directions of each
road, so the sum of the distances is divided by 2:

```{r}
por_arestas <- grafo |>
  dplyr::filter(component > 1) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    arestas = dplyr::n(),
    km      = sum(d) / 2 / 1000,
    .by = component
  )
```

Now, the three together, and the likely cause, by the rules in the table above. `case_when()` tests the
rules in order and keeps the first one that holds:

```{r}
resumo <- por_vertices |>
  dplyr::left_join(por_linhas,  by = "component") |>
  dplyr::left_join(por_arestas, by = "component") |>
  dplyr::mutate(causa = dplyr::case_when(
    dist_borda_m < 500     ~ "Cut at the edge",
    dist_principal_m < 5   ~ "Near-coincident ends",
    dist_principal_m < 300 ~ "Road outside the profile or download",
    cruzamentos > 0        ~ "Crosses without a node",
    TRUE                   ~ "Isolated"
  )) |>
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(arestas))

resumo |>
  dplyr::select(component, arestas, km, vias, dist_principal_m, dist_borda_m, causa) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 1, format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
               col.names = c("Component", "Edges", "km", "Roads", "Dist. to main (m)",
                             "Dist. to edge (m)", "Likely cause"))
```

```{r}
resumo |>
  dplyr::summarise(pedacos = dplyr::n(), arestas = sum(arestas), km = sum(km), .by = causa) |>
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(arestas)) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 1,
               col.names = c("Likely cause", "Pieces", "Edges", "km"))
```

On the map, the loose pieces coloured by cause, over the roads of the main component within
1 km of them. Hover over a segment to see the component and the distance:

```{r}
cores_causa <- c("Cut at the edge" = "#7A1F0F", "Near-coincident ends" = "#E7A07A",
                 "Road outside the profile or download" = "#C2542D", "Crosses without a node" = "#2F6B9A",
                 "Isolated" = "#173A57")
cores_causa <- cores_causa[names(cores_causa) %in% resumo$causa]

causas <- dplyr::select(resumo, component, causa, dist_principal_m)

soltos_mapa <- linhas_soltas |>
  dplyr::left_join(causas, by = "component") |>
  dplyr::mutate(rotulo = paste0("component ", component, ": ", causa, " (",
                                round(dist_principal_m), " m from the main one)")) |>
  sf::st_transform(4326)

perto <- sf::st_is_within_distance(linhas_principal, linhas_soltas, dist = 1000)
contexto <- linhas_principal[lengths(perto) > 0, ] |> sf::st_transform(4326)

mapa_base(soltos_mapa) |>
  mapgl::add_line_layer(id = "borda", source = borda_mapa,
                        line_color = "#333333", line_width = 1.5, line_dasharray = c(2, 2)) |>
  mapgl::add_line_layer(id = "principal", source = contexto,
                        line_color = "#9a9a9a", line_width = 1.5) |>
  mapgl::add_line_layer(
    id = "soltos", source = soltos_mapa, line_width = 4, tooltip = "rotulo",
    line_color = mapgl::match_expr("causa", values = names(cores_causa),
                                   stops = unname(cores_causa))
  ) |>
  mapgl::add_legend("Likely cause", values = names(cores_causa),
                    colors = unname(cores_causa), type = "categorical")
```

### Up close: one piece of each cause

Zooming in on one example of each cause, with a dashed line between the point of the loose piece and the
nearest vertex of the main component:

```{r}
mapa_detalhe <- function(comp) {
  pedaco <- dplyr::filter(soltos_mapa, component == comp)
  # the closest pair of vertices: one from the loose piece, one from the main component
  par  <- dplyr::filter(soltos, component == comp) |> dplyr::slice_min(dist_principal, n = 1)
  alvo <- dplyr::filter(principal, id == par$id_principal)
  ponta_a <- sf::st_coordinates(sf::st_transform(par, 4326))
  ponta_b <- sf::st_coordinates(sf::st_transform(alvo, 4326))
  ligacao <- sf::st_sf(
    distancia = paste(round(par$dist_principal, 1), "m"),
    geometry  = sf::st_sfc(sf::st_linestring(rbind(ponta_a, ponta_b)), crs = 4326)
  )
  janela <- sf::st_buffer(sf::st_transform(pedaco, crs_metrico), 400) |>
    sf::st_union() |>
    sf::st_transform(4326)
  vizinhas <- contexto[lengths(sf::st_intersects(contexto, janela)) > 0, ]

  mapa_base(janela, altura = "380px") |>
    mapgl::add_line_layer(id = paste0("p", comp), source = vizinhas,
                          line_color = "#9a9a9a", line_width = 2, tooltip = "highway") |>
    mapgl::add_line_layer(id = paste0("s", comp), source = pedaco, line_width = 5,
                          line_color = unname(cores_causa[pedaco$causa[1]]), tooltip = "rotulo") |>
    mapgl::add_line_layer(id = paste0("l", comp), source = ligacao, line_color = "#000000",
                          line_width = 2, line_dasharray = c(1, 1), tooltip = "distancia")
}

exemplos <- resumo |> dplyr::slice_max(arestas, n = 1, by = causa)
```

```{r}
# one map per example, each with a title
htmltools::tagList(lapply(seq_len(nrow(exemplos)), function(i) {
  htmltools::tagList(
    htmltools::tags$p(htmltools::tags$strong(exemplos$causa[i]),
                      sprintf(" (component %d, %s km, %s m from the main one)",
                              exemplos$component[i],
                              format(round(exemplos$km[i], 1)),
                              format(round(exemplos$dist_principal_m[i], 1)))),
    mapa_detalhe(exemplos$component[i])
  )
}))
```

What the examples show:

- **Near-coincident ends**: the loose road ends a few metres from another, but OSM does not
  have the meeting node. It is a mapping error, and a connector a few metres long solves it.
- **Road outside the profile or download**: the loose stretch would connect to the rest through a
  `tertiary` or local road, which was not downloaded. The real fix is to include those road
  types in the OSM query; the connector is a stopgap.
- **Cut at the edge**: the road leaves the rectangle and comes back, or only connects to the rest outside it.
  Download OSM with a margin of a few kilometres and crop only the results.
- **Isolated**: far from everything. Either you accept a long connector, or you discard it.

## 4. Quick fix: only the main component

In most studies, this is enough. Origin and destination points are then linked to the
nearest vertex of the connected network:

```{r}
grafo_principal <- grafo[grafo$component == 1, ]

c(arestas_antes = nrow(grafo), arestas_depois = nrow(grafo_principal),
  km_descartados = round(sum(resumo$km), 1))
```

## 5. One-way streets: you can go, but you cannot come back

`component` says whether the pieces **touch**, not whether it is possible to go and come back respecting the
direction of the roads. That is what **strongly connected components** are for: within one, from any
vertex you can reach any other. A vertex outside the largest strong component is a place you
can reach but cannot leave (a dead end), or the reverse: the route gives `NA`, with no error.

```{r}
g_igraph <- dodgr::dodgr_to_igraph(grafo_principal)
fortes   <- igraph::components(g_igraph, mode = "strong")
ids_fortes <- names(fortes$membership)[fortes$membership == which.max(fortes$csize)]

presos <- setdiff(igraph::V(g_igraph)$name, ids_fortes)

c(componentes_fortes = fortes$no,
  vertices_presos    = length(presos),
  pct_presos         = round(100 * length(presos) / igraph::vcount(g_igraph), 1))
```

For each trapped vertex, we test whether it can be reached from the core, and whether one can
get back from it to the core:

```{r}
um_do_nucleo <- which(igraph::V(g_igraph)$name == ids_fortes[1])
ida   <- igraph::distances(g_igraph, v = um_do_nucleo, to = presos, mode = "out")
volta <- igraph::distances(g_igraph, v = um_do_nucleo, to = presos, mode = "in")

v_presos <- vertices |>
  dplyr::filter(id %in% presos) |>
  dplyr::left_join(data.frame(id = presos, entra = is.finite(ida[1, ]),
                              sai = is.finite(volta[1, ])), by = "id") |>
  dplyr::mutate(tipo = dplyr::case_when(
    entra & !sai ~ "Sink: in but not out",
    !entra & sai ~ "Source: out but not in",
    TRUE         ~ "Neither in nor out"
  ))
v_presos$dist_borda <- dist_borda(v_presos)

dplyr::count(sf::st_drop_geometry(v_presos), tipo, sort = TRUE)

# near the edge? and on what type of road?
round(100 * mean(v_presos$dist_borda < 1000))       # % less than 1 km from the edge
grafo_principal |>
  dplyr::filter(from_id %in% presos | to_id %in% presos) |>
  dplyr::count(highway, sort = TRUE) |>
  head(6)
```

On the map, each trapped vertex, coloured by type. Zoom in on a slip road or an
interchange to see the pattern:

```{r}
cores_tipo <- c("Sink: in but not out" = "#C2542D", "Source: out but not in" = "#2F6B9A",
                "Neither in nor out" = "#7A7A7A")

presos_mapa <- v_presos |>
  dplyr::select(id, tipo) |>
  sf::st_transform(4326)

mapa_base(presos_mapa) |>
  mapgl::add_line_layer(id = "borda2", source = borda_mapa,
                        line_color = "#333333", line_width = 1.5, line_dasharray = c(2, 2)) |>
  mapgl::add_circle_layer(
    id = "presos", source = presos_mapa, circle_radius = 2.5, circle_opacity = 0.8,
    circle_color = mapgl::match_expr("tipo", values = names(cores_tipo),
                                     stops = unname(cores_tipo)),
    tooltip = "tipo"
  ) |>
  mapgl::add_legend("Vertices trapped by one-way streets", values = names(cores_tipo),
                    colors = unname(cores_tipo), type = "categorical")
```

Most trapped vertices are far from the edge, on slip roads (`_link`) and secondary roads. The
likely hypothesis is that the way back depends on roads that were not downloaded: the same problem as in
section 3, now with direction of travel. The routing solution is to keep only the strong core:

```{r}
grafo_forte <- grafo_principal[grafo_principal$from_id %in% ids_fortes &
                               grafo_principal$to_id   %in% ids_fortes, ]
nrow(grafo_forte)
```

## 6. Crossings without a node: datasets outside OSM

In OSM, roads that cross at grade share a node; those that cross without a node are
overpasses and tunnels, and must **not** be connected. On this network,
`r sum(linhas_soltas$cruza)` loose segments cross the main component without a node, and those are such cases.

In datasets such as DNIT's SNV or your own *shapefile*, however, lines often cross without a
shared vertex, and the graph comes out all chopped up. A minimal example, with two roads in an X:

```{r}
x_sem_no <- sf::st_sf(
  osm_id  = c("a", "b"), highway = c("primary", "secondary"), oneway = "no",
  geometry = sf::st_sfc(sf::st_linestring(rbind(c(-46.34, -23.96), c(-46.32, -23.94))),
                        sf::st_linestring(rbind(c(-46.34, -23.94), c(-46.32, -23.96))),
                        crs = 4326))

dodgr::weight_streetnet(x_sem_no, wt_profile = "motorcar", type_col = "highway",
                        id_col = "osm_id")$component |> table()
```

Two components: the roads cross, but the graph does not know it. The function below creates a node at each
crossing and snaps ends less than 5 m apart:

```{r}
nodar_linhas <- function(linhas, tolerancia_m = 5, crs = crs_metrico) {
  linhas <- sf::st_transform(linhas, crs)
  linhas <- sf::st_snap(linhas, linhas, tolerance = tolerancia_m)   # joins nearby ends

  # st_node() creates a node at each crossing; st_cast() separates the pieces between nodes
  pedacos <- linhas |>
    sf::st_union() |>
    sf::st_node() |>
    sf::st_cast("LINESTRING") |>
    sf::st_sf(geometry = _)

  # each piece inherits the attributes of the original line it lies on (by its midpoint)
  meio   <- sf::st_cast(sf::st_line_sample(pedacos, sample = 0.5), "POINT")
  origem <- sf::st_nearest_feature(meio, linhas)
  pedacos <- sf::st_sf(sf::st_drop_geometry(linhas)[origem, , drop = FALSE],
                       geometry = sf::st_geometry(pedacos))
  pedacos$osm_id <- paste0(pedacos$osm_id, "_", seq_len(nrow(pedacos)))   # unique ids
  sf::st_transform(pedacos, 4326)
}

x_nodado <- nodar_linhas(x_sem_no)
x_nodado

dodgr::weight_streetnet(x_nodado, wt_profile = "motorcar", type_col = "highway",
                        id_col = "osm_id")$component |> table()
```

A single component, with four segments meeting at the crossing. Do not apply this to an
OSM network: it would connect every overpass to the road below.

## 7. Reconnecting the loose pieces

When you do not want to lose the pieces, you create a **link edge** (in both directions)
between each loose piece and the nearest vertex of the main component. A distance limit prevents
absurd links, and a penalty makes routing avoid using the connector as a shortcut:

```{r}
reconectar_componentes <- function(grafo, limite_m = 300, penalidade = 3, vel_kmh = 20) {
  v <- dodgr::dodgr_vertices(grafo) |>
    sf::st_as_sf(coords = c("x", "y"), crs = 4326, remove = FALSE) |>
    sf::st_transform(crs_metrico)
  principal <- v[v$component == 1, ]
  soltos    <- v[v$component > 1, ]
  if (nrow(soltos) == 0) return(grafo)

  idx <- sf::st_nearest_feature(soltos, principal)
  soltos$to_id  <- principal$id[idx]
  soltos$to_lon <- principal$x[idx]
  soltos$to_lat <- principal$y[idx]
  soltos$d      <- as.numeric(sf::st_distance(soltos, principal[idx, ], by_element = TRUE))

  # one link per piece: the closest pair of vertices, within the limit
  lig <- soltos |>
    sf::st_drop_geometry() |>
    dplyr::slice_min(d, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE, by = component) |>
    dplyr::filter(d <= limite_m)
  if (nrow(lig) == 0) return(grafo)

  ida <- data.frame(from_id = lig$id,    from_lon = lig$x,      from_lat = lig$y,
                    to_id   = lig$to_id, to_lon   = lig$to_lon, to_lat   = lig$to_lat,
                    d = lig$d)
  volta <- data.frame(from_id = ida$to_id,   from_lon = ida$to_lon,   from_lat = ida$to_lat,
                      to_id   = ida$from_id, to_lon   = ida$from_lon, to_lat   = ida$from_lat,
                      d = ida$d)

  novas <- dplyr::bind_rows(ida, volta) |>
    dplyr::mutate(
      d             = pmax(d, 1),              # coincident ends: 1 m, never zero
      d_weighted    = d * penalidade,          # discourages using the connector
      highway       = "conector",
      time          = d / (vel_kmh / 3.6),
      time_weighted = time * penalidade
    )
  novas$edge_id <- max(grafo$edge_id) + seq_len(nrow(novas))

  saida <- dplyr::bind_rows(as.data.frame(grafo), novas)
  saida$component <- NULL
  saida <- dodgr::dodgr_components(saida)      # recomputes: component 1 is the largest again
  class(saida) <- class(grafo)                 # gives back the dodgr class
  attr(saida, "wt_profile") <- attr(grafo, "wt_profile")
  saida
}
```

The function runs until the number of components stops changing: a piece far from the main component may
end up close to another that has just been connected.

```{r}
grafo_rec <- grafo
rodadas <- c(length(unique(grafo_rec$component)))
repeat {
  grafo_rec <- reconectar_componentes(grafo_rec, limite_m = 300)
  rodadas <- c(rodadas, length(unique(grafo_rec$component)))
  if (rodadas[length(rodadas)] == rodadas[length(rodadas) - 1]) break
}
rodadas                                   # components after each round

conectores <- grafo_rec[grafo_rec$highway == "conector", ]
c(conectores = nrow(conectores) / 2, maior_m = round(max(conectores$d)))
```

On the map, the connectors created (in black) and the pieces they link. Notice how almost all of them
are very short:

```{r}
conectores_sf <- conectores |>
  dplyr::filter(from_id < to_id) |>           # one per pair (there and back are the same stroke)
  dplyr::mutate(geometry = sf::st_sfc(
    lapply(seq_len(dplyr::n()), \(i) sf::st_linestring(rbind(c(from_lon[i], from_lat[i]),
                                                             c(to_lon[i], to_lat[i])))),
    crs = 4326),
    rotulo = paste(round(d), "m")) |>
  sf::st_as_sf()

mapa_base(soltos_mapa) |>
  mapgl::add_line_layer(id = "principal3", source = contexto,
                        line_color = "#9a9a9a", line_width = 1.5) |>
  mapgl::add_line_layer(id = "soltos3", source = soltos_mapa, line_width = 4,
                        line_color = mapgl::match_expr("causa", values = names(cores_causa),
                                                       stops = unname(cores_causa))) |>
  mapgl::add_line_layer(id = "conectores", source = conectores_sf, line_color = "#000000",
                        line_width = 4, tooltip = "rotulo") |>
  mapgl::add_circle_layer(id = "conectores_ponta", source = sf::st_cast(conectores_sf, "POINT"),
                          circle_color = "#000000", circle_radius = 3)
```

Three precautions:

- **The penalty matters.** Without it, a route may use the connector as a shortcut. When measuring
  accessibility, it is worth reporting how many routes go through a connector.
- **One-way streets are not solved here.** The connector is two-way, but the piece may be one-way
  inside; the next section shows how many remain.
- **The connector is a stopgap.** It hides a flaw in the network; the real fix, when
  possible, is to download or repair the missing road.

## 8. Checking: routes before and after

Two samples of points, routed on five versions of the graph: 300 vertices drawn at random across the
network, and one vertex from each loose piece. The question is simple: for how many pairs is there no route?

```{r}
so_o_forte <- function(g) {
  g1 <- g[g$component == 1, ]
  f  <- igraph::components(dodgr::dodgr_to_igraph(g1), mode = "strong")
  ids <- names(f$membership)[f$membership == which.max(f$csize)]
  g1[g1$from_id %in% ids & g1$to_id %in% ids, ]
}

grafos <- list(
  "Original"                     = grafo,
  "Main only"                    = grafo_principal,
  "Main only, strong core"       = grafo_forte,
  "Reconnected"                  = grafo_rec,
  "Reconnected, strong core"     = so_o_forte(grafo_rec)
)

set.seed(42)
amostra_rede   <- vertices |> sf::st_drop_geometry() |> dplyr::slice_sample(n = 300)
amostra_soltos <- soltos   |> sf::st_drop_geometry() |> dplyr::slice_sample(n = 1, by = component)

sem_rota <- function(g, pts) {
  pts <- as.matrix(pts[, c("x", "y")])
  m <- dodgr::dodgr_dists(g, from = pts, to = pts)
  100 * mean(is.na(m[row(m) != col(m)]))
}

comparacao <- data.frame(
  grafo   = names(grafos),
  arestas = vapply(grafos, nrow, integer(1)),
  rede    = vapply(grafos, sem_rota, numeric(1), pts = amostra_rede),
  soltos  = vapply(grafos, sem_rota, numeric(1), pts = amostra_soltos),
  row.names = NULL
)

comparacao |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 1, format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
               col.names = c("Graph", "Edges", "No route: whole network (%)",
                             "No route: loose pieces (%)"))
```

```{r}
ids_nucleo_rec <- unique(c(grafos[["Reconnected, strong core"]]$from_id,
                           grafos[["Reconnected, strong core"]]$to_id))
recuperados <- soltos |>
  sf::st_drop_geometry() |>
  dplyr::summarise(no_nucleo = mean(id %in% ids_nucleo_rec), .by = component)
```

In a pruned graph, a point that was in a discarded piece is linked to the nearest
vertex that remains, and so it gets a route; the distance of that "jump" is left out of the calculation.

## What this network teaches

- There are `r nrow(resumo)` **loose pieces**, with
  `r format(round(sum(resumo$km), 1))` km of road. The most common cause is a
  link through a road that was not downloaded: the network only has roads up to `secondary`.
- **One-way streets** are the bigger problem: `r format(length(presos), big.mark = ",")` vertices
  (`r format(round(100 * length(presos) / igraph::vcount(g_igraph), 1))`%)
  are outside the core where you can go and come back, and they are what make the route come out `NA`.
- **Reconnecting** joins the pieces into a single component, but only
  `r sum(recuperados$no_nucleo >= 0.5)` of the `r nrow(recuperados)` get a way there and back: the
  connector does not solve one-way streets.
- To route on this network, the solution that brings the pairs with no route down to zero is the **strong core**, with the
  points linked to it.
- To lose no piece at all, the way is the source of the problem: also download the
  `tertiary` and `tertiary_link` roads and repeat this diagnosis. This page did not test that
  hypothesis; it is the natural exercise to settle it.

The same routine works for any network: build the graph, count the weak and the
strong components, put the loose pieces on a map, and only then choose the fix.
